issues.legal_issue: Rejecting eyewitness testimony because it conflicts with a dying declaration does not by itself make the dying declaration unreliable.
material_facts: The trial court rejected the eyewitnesses as unreliable and treated their conflict with the dying declaration as a reason to reject the declaration as well.
The Supreme Court found the declaration coherent, consistent, and reliable, and agreed that it could sustain the conviction despite the rejection of the eyewitness testimony.
issues.conclusion: The trial court erred in treating the rejection of the conflicting eyewitness testimony as a reason to reject the dying declaration; the declaration could be assessed independently.
issues.legal_principle: The reliability of a dying declaration must be assessed on its own merits. A conflict between it and eyewitness testimony does not necessarily make the declaration unreliable. Section 32(1) of the Indian Evidence Act gives qualifying statements about the cause or circumstances of death relevance; Khushal Rao v. State of Bombay was relied on for the special evidentiary status of such declarations.

predicates.criminal_case_based_on_dying_declaration: The proceeding is a criminal case in which a dying declaration is relied on as evidence.
predicates.eyewitness_testimony_rejected_as_inconsi: The court rejects eyewitness testimony because it conflicts with the dying declaration.
predicates.declaration_independently_coherent: The dying declaration is coherent when assessed independently.

issues.definition: When a criminal case relies on a coherent dying declaration and conflicting eyewitness testimony is rejected, the conflict alone does not make the declaration unreliable.

issues.legal_issue: A dying declaration is not unsafe merely because the declarant was described as being in shock when the evidence shows that the declarant retained the capacity to make a coherent statement.
material_facts: The doctor who recorded the declaration said the deceased was in shock from a serious abdominal injury.
The doctor was not cross-examined on whether the deceased retained his mental faculties despite the shock.
The declaration was coherent and consistent, and the doctor recorded that the patient became semi-conscious toward its end.
issues.conclusion: The evidence did not establish that the deceased lacked his mental faculties when he began making the declaration, and the shock ground did not make the declaration unsafe to rely on.
issues.legal_principle: A medical condition such as shock must be assessed in light of evidence about the declarant’s actual mental state. A medical-jurisprudence view relied on by a party must be put to the doctor in cross-examination so its application to the particular facts can be assessed.

rule.if: dying_declaration_case and declarant_described_as_in_shock and coherent_statement_before_later_decline and doctor_not_questioned_on_retained_faculties

predicates.dying_declaration_case: The proceeding concerns the evidentiary reliability of a dying declaration.
predicates.declarant_described_as_in_shock: A medical witness describes the declarant as being in shock.
predicates.coherent_statement_before_later_decline: The declarant makes a coherent statement before becoming semi-conscious or otherwise declining.
predicates.doctor_not_questioned_on_retained_facult: The medical witness is not questioned about whether the declarant retained mental faculties despite the shock.

issues.definition: In a dying-declaration case, shock alone does not make a declaration unsafe when the declarant made a coherent statement before a later decline and the doctor was not questioned about retained faculties.

issues.legal_issue: A medical-jurisprudence opinion about a patient’s mental condition should be put to the doctor before it is relied on to assess the declarant’s capacity in the particular case.
material_facts: The defence relied on a medical-jurisprudence passage stating that shock after violence may cause a dying person’s intellect to become confused.
The doctor who recorded the declaration was not asked in cross-examination about that opinion or whether it applied to the deceased.
issues.conclusion: The Court would not rely on the medical-jurisprudence observations because they had not been put to the doctor for assessment in the circumstances of the case.
issues.legal_principle: When a party relies on a particular view expressed by medical-jurisprudence authors, that view must be put to the doctor so the doctor can assess how far it applies to the facts of the case.

predicates.medical_evidence_case: The proceeding involves medical evidence relevant to a factual assessment.
predicates.party_relies_on_medical_textbook_opinion: A party relies on an opinion from a medical-jurisprudence text.
predicates.opinion_not_put_to_doctor: The opinion is not put to the doctor for assessment in relation to the facts of the case.

issues.definition: When a party relies on a medical-jurisprudence opinion in a case involving medical evidence, the opinion is not used for a case-specific assessment if it was not put to the doctor.

issues.legal_issue: A dying declaration is not incomplete merely because the declarant cannot answer a final, formal question after already giving the full account.
material_facts: The doctor asked the deceased what more he wanted to say after the deceased had narrated the account of the occurrence.
The deceased could not answer because he became semi-conscious.
The Court found that the doctor had asked the necessary questions and that the final question was merely formal.
issues.conclusion: The declaration was not incomplete because the deceased had already narrated the full story and could not answer only the final formal question.
issues.legal_principle: Whether a dying declaration is incomplete depends on whether the declarant left the account unfinished in a material way. The Court distinguished Cyril Waugh v. The King, where the declarant could not complete the main sentence describing the genesis and motive of the occurrence.

rule.if: dying_declaration_case and full_account_already_given and final_question_merely_formal and inability_to_answer_after_account

predicates.dying_declaration_case: The proceeding concerns whether a dying declaration is complete enough to be relied on.
predicates.full_account_already_given: The declarant has already given the full account relevant to the occurrence.
predicates.final_question_merely_formal: The unanswered question merely invites the declarant to add anything further and does not seek an outstanding material part of the account.
predicates.inability_to_answer_after_account: The declarant cannot answer the final question after giving the account.

issues.definition: A dying declaration is not incomplete when the full account has been given and the declarant cannot answer only a final, formal invitation to add more.

issues.legal_issue: The fact that a dying declaration names additional persons who are not prosecuted does not by itself establish that the declaration is false.
material_facts: The deceased named persons in addition to the appellants as participants in the assault.
Those additional persons were not charge-sheeted.
The Court considered that their omission from the prosecution could have resulted from ulterior motives and did not by itself undermine the declaration.
issues.conclusion: The non-prosecution of additional persons named in the declaration did not, by itself, prove that the declaration was false.
issues.legal_principle: A dying declaration must be assessed on its evidentiary merits; the omission from prosecution of persons named in it does not alone establish falsity. Section 32(1) of the Indian Evidence Act recognizes relevant statements about the cause or circumstances of death.

predicates.dying_declaration_case: The proceeding concerns the truth or reliability of a dying declaration.
predicates.declaration_names_additional_persons: The dying declaration names persons in addition to those prosecuted.
predicates.additional_persons_not_prosecuted: The additional persons named in the declaration are not prosecuted.

issues.definition: When a dying declaration names additional persons who are not prosecuted, that non-prosecution alone does not establish that the declaration is false.

issues.legal_issue: A true, carefully scrutinized, coherent, consistent, and unprompted dying declaration may by itself support a criminal conviction without corroboration.
material_facts: The High Court relied on the declaration after rejecting the eyewitness testimony.
The Supreme Court found the declaration straightforward, rational, coherent, consistent, and free from any indication of prompting or tutoring.
The declaration described the motive and participants, and the Court found it true and reliable.
issues.conclusion: The declaration was sufficient to sustain the conviction even without corroboration, and the appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 32(1) of the Indian Evidence Act makes a qualifying dying declaration a relevant fact and gives it special evidentiary status. Under Khushal Rao v. State of Bombay, Tarachand Damu Sutar v. State of Maharashtra, and Mannu Raja v. State of Madhya Pradesh, a true dying declaration may support a conviction without corroboration after careful scrutiny. Ram Nath Madhoprasad v. State of Madhya Pradesh was overruled to the extent it required corroboration.

predicates.declaration_carefully_scrutinized: The court carefully scrutinizes the dying declaration.

predicates.declaration_coherent_and_consistent: The declaration is coherent and consistent.

issues.definition: In a criminal case, a carefully scrutinized, true, coherent, consistent, and unprompted dying declaration may alone support a conviction without corroboration.
